Let’s dive into Chapter 1: Two Paths of Leadership—Multipliers and Diminishers.
Think about the leaders you’ve worked with. Some just seem to light a spark in their teams—people get creative, dig deeper, and grow every day. Others, even if they mean well, somehow leave their teams feeling underused or even drained.
What’s really going on here? It all comes down to two very different ways of leading. Multipliers and Diminishers.
Multipliers are those leaders who actually amplify the intelligence and energy of everyone around them. They don’t see themselves as the only source of answers—instead, they look at their teams and see a well of talent and insight. Their actions invite people to stretch, learn, and really show what they’re capable of.
Now, Diminishers—they often don’t even realize the effect they’re having. They might be smart and talented themselves, but their style leaves others feeling less trusted, less capable, and a lot less likely to speak up with their best ideas.
It’s not just about intent or personality; it’s about habits and beliefs. Multipliers act on the idea that people are smart and, if given the room, they’ll figure things out. Diminishers may think only a few people really have what it takes, or that they’re the ones who need to be in control—so they micromanage, or overshadow, even when they don’t mean to.
Here’s why this matters: Teams led by Multipliers consistently outperform those led by Diminishers—not because the leader’s the smartest person in the room, but because the whole team’s intelligence is in play. When Diminishers are in charge, so much talent goes to waste, morale drops, and new ideas just don’t get off the ground.
Picture a garden for a second. A Multiplier is like a gardener who enriches the soil and gives plants what they need, then trusts them to grow strong. A Diminisher? Well, that’s the person who keeps yanking up the plants to check their roots—never giving them a real chance to flourish.
The real key is being able to spot these patterns. Even the most well-meaning leaders can slip into diminishing behaviors without realizing it. Becoming a Multiplier starts with a little self-awareness and a willingness to notice how your actions make others grow—or shrink.
This whole framework is built around five core disciplines that define what Multipliers do differently. These aren’t just for CEOs or managers—they’re for anyone who leads, whether you have a title or not.
And before we get into those five disciplines, here’s something important: Being a Multiplier isn’t about being hands-off or just letting things happen. It’s about creating the right conditions—where people are challenged, supported, and trusted to bring their best. It’s an intentional way to lead, one that makes everyone around you smarter and stronger.
